beats.vo: A tube. A spiral. And water that climbs uphill... by itself.
This is the Archimedes screw. Twenty-three centuries old... and still in use today.
Here's the trick. Tilt it to thirty degrees.
Turn it... and every pocket of water gets trapped between the blades.
The screw turns. The pocket can't fall back... so it climbs.
No pump. No pressure. Just geometry.
Archimedes used it to drain a ship the size of a palace.
And today, cities run it in reverse. Water flows down... and the screw makes electricity.
Twenty-three centuries... and we never found anything better.
Should I rebuild the Roman crane next... or the pyramid's hidden ramp? Comment A or B.

metadata.title: This 2,300-Year-Old Machine Still Powers Cities 🌀 #AncientTech
metadata.description:
The Archimedes screw: tilt a spiral to ~30°, turn it, and every pocket of water is trapped and forced uphill — no pump, no pressure, just geometry. Today it runs in reverse as a hydro turbine.

3D reconstruction by Ancient Tech. Comment A or B to pick the next build.

Sources: Vitruvius X.6; Rorres, 'The Turn of the Screw' (2000).
